Chagatai Khan was the second son of Genghis Khan and his chief wife, Börte. Born around 1184, he reigned over the territory that would later become the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia until his death in 1242.

👑 Biography and Military Campaigns

Chagatai Khan was a key figure in his father's early military expansions.

  • Early Life and Personality: Though some Mongols considered him a strong candidate to succeed his father, Genghis Khan ultimately excluded Chagatai from the succession to the position of Great Khan. Genghis felt he was too strict and narrow-minded, exhibiting an inflexibility unsuitable for a supreme ruler. This inflexibility was also seen in his strict adherence to traditional Mongol law (Yassa).
  • The Khwarazmian Campaign: Chagatai played a crucial role during the Mongol conquest of the Khwarazmian Empire.
    • He commanded forces alongside his brother Ögedei at the Siege of Otrar (1219–1220), leading to the capture and execution of the governor, Inalchuq.
    • He then participated in the lengthy Siege of Gurganj. Historical accounts often claim he quarreled with his older brother, Jochi, over how to conduct the siege, leading Genghis Khan to promote Ögedei to command. However, some modern historians argue this narrative of fraternal conflict was a later invention intended to solidify Ögedei’s right to rule.
  • Personal Loss: During the siege of Bamiyan in 1221, Chagatai’s favorite son, Mutukan, was killed. At the request of Mutukan's widow, Genghis Khan ordered the entire population of Bamiyan to be massacred in revenge.

⚖️ Succession and Rule in Central Asia

Despite being excluded from the Great Khanate, Chagatai was given his own appanage (or ulus), which grew into the Chagatai Khanate.

  • The Great Khan's Successor: Due to the tensions with his half-brother Jochi, whom Chagatai publicly called a "Merkit bastard," and his own unyielding nature, Genghis Khan passed over both Chagatai and Jochi, naming Ögedei Khan as his chosen successor to the Mongol Empire.
  • Ruler of the Khanate: After Genghis Khan's death in 1227, Chagatai established his territory in Central Asia, though he often clashed with the officials Ögedei appointed to the region. He frequently squabbled with the Muslim administrator Mahmud Yalavach over jurisdictional control, forcing Ögedei to intervene to resolve the tense situation.
  • Death and Political Influence: Chagatai died in 1242, shortly after Ögedei's death. He was a kingmaker in the political turmoil following Ögedei’s death, lending his crucial support to Ögedei's wife, Töregene, allowing her to become regent.

🗿 Legacy and Reputation

Chagatai was a capable ruler who recruited foreign experts and local Uighur officials to administer his realm. However, he left a complex historical reputation.

  • The Yassa vs. Sharia: Chagatai was known for his strict adherence to the traditional Mongol Yassa (law), which often stood in direct contradiction to elements of Islamic Sharia law. Specifically, he strictly forbade:
    • Islamic animal slaughter (dhabihah).
    • Ritual hygiene (wudu).
    • Public prayer (Salah).
  • Anti-Muslim Reputation: Because of his enforcement of the Yassa over these Muslim practices, he gained a contemporary reputation, documented by writers like Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani, for being intensely anti-Muslim.
  • Modern Historical View: Modern historians, such as Michael Hope and Devin DeWeese, view this reputation more as evidence of Chagatai being a conservative Mongol traditionalist who upheld the laws established by his father, rather than a ruler driven purely by religious intolerance.

He was succeeded in the Khanate by his grandson, Qara Hülegü. The territories he ruled were named the Chagatai Khanate in his honor.
